title: Foreign tourists may soon travel across Nepal using immigration app - National Herald
description: Foreign tourists may soon travel across Nepal using immigration app  National Herald
publisher.title: National Herald
full_article:
Nepal is preparing a mobile-based system allowing foreign visitors to travel within the country without routinely carrying their physical passports

Tourists will be able to store passport and visa details on an official immigration app and use them for domestic flights, hotel check-ins and other services

The initiative will be linked to a nationwide database that tracks foreign nationals from their visa application until their departure from Nepal

Foreign visitors may soon be able to travel within Nepal without routinely carrying their physical passports under a digital initiative being developed by the country’s Department of Immigration.

The proposed “Passport-Free Travel” arrangement will allow foreign nationals to store scanned copies of their passports and visa details on the department’s official mobile application.

After arriving in Nepal, visitors will have to install the app and submit the required information. Once their details have been registered and verified, they will be able to use the digital records while travelling within the country.

“Then they can freely travel across the country without carrying their physical passports,” Department of Immigration director general Ram Chandra Tiwari said.

The application is available on Android and Apple’s iOS platform, according to the department.

Under the planned system, registered foreigners will not be required to present their physical passports when boarding domestic flights, checking into hotels, exchanging currency or arranging trips through travel and trekking agencies.

“For example, they may forget their passport at a hotel while travelling and be unable to produce it when required,” Tiwari said. “By updating their information on the app, they will no longer have to worry about forgetting their passport at a hotel or elsewhere while they are inside Nepal.”

publisher.title: VnExpress International
full_article:
The 50-year-old mountaineer felt unwell as he was descending from Camp II after an acclimatization rotation.

"He passed away this morning, arrangements have been made to airlift his body," Pemba Sherpa of 8K Expeditions told AFP .

This season, 480 climbers are attempting to reach the summit of the 8,163-meter (26,781-feet) high mountain in Nepal.

A view of the Manaslu Circuit Trek. Illustration photo by Unsplash

This month, a 20-year-old Nepali porter was found dead in his tent at the mountain's base camp.

The Singaporean climber was the first foreign fatality of the autumn climbing season.

Autumn expeditions on the Himalayas are less popular because of the shorter, colder days, snowy terrain and a narrow summit window compared to the busy spring.

Nepal has issued 536 permits for nine peaks, a little over a half of the total permits issued in spring.

Nepal is home to eight of the world's 14 highest peaks and foreign climbers that flock to its mountains are a major source of revenue for the country.

Fears for the industry rose after a devastating flood hit Nepal late August, but expedition organizers say most climbers have not cancelled their expeditions.

title: Why WFP calls Nepal flood relief one of its toughest missions | Explained - The Hindu
description: Why WFP calls Nepal flood relief one of its toughest missions | Explained  The Hindu
publisher.title: The Hindu
full_article:
The story so far: Weeks after catastrophic floods hit Nepal, authorities are scrambling to mount a relief effort with over 6,000 people still missing and death toll climbing to 1,410. Aid operations in the disaster-hit country rank among the most challenging for the World Food Programme (WFP), its head said on Thursday (September 17, 2026).

What has the WFP said?

Riaz Lodhi, head of the WFP in Nepal, said that the August 26 flash floods and its aftermath were among the “top three most challenging disasters” the agency had faced. The WFP, a branch of the United Nations which is committed to ending hunger and has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, provides relief in conflict and disaster zones.

While speaking about the Nepal situation, Mr. Lodhi cited the profound access challenge in the country. “We have seen disasters, we have seen earthquakes, we have seen disasters caused by floods, we have seen war situations, conflicts,” he told AFP. “We have had access challenges in many of these situations”, he added, but said the challenges in Nepal were extreme.

What are the challenges WFP faces?

Workers unload emergency relief supplies from the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) for flash flood victims at Tribhuvan International Airport's cargo area in Kathmandu on September 17, 2026. | Photo Credit: AFP

The flooding and landslides have displaced several people and have disrupted access to essential services. The WFP has said that the main operational constraint has been physical access to affected people. Several areas in the epicenter of the disaster remain cut off. A largely rural country, many people in Nepal live in mountain districts. The flash flood, reportedly triggered by a Himalayan glacial mountain collapse, wiped away key access points. Around 40 bridges have been damaged or destroyed and the risk of flooding persists making the terrain unstable. Mudslides and rubble have also hampered relief efforts.

Nepal wants climate compensation, putting major emitters on the hook

Rasuwa and Nuwakot remain among the worst-affected areas. In Rasuwa, several communities are only reachable through air travel. “This is a very unique access challenge where, in some places, the only way to reach people is by helicopter,” Mr. Lodhi said.

Apart from being an expensive endeavor, the time taken to reach these places has also now increased. Rebuilding the necessary infrastructure is expected to take several weeks.

What is being done now?

The Nepal government is working with the UN to help those affected by the deadly disaster. Relief supplies are being dispatched continuously by road and air while temporary bridges are being set up where necessary. Army Personnel are also using temporary zip lines to transport people from one river bank to another. The WFP has said that it is using drones to provide food to affected people. These drones can reportedly carry up to 100kg, depending on the operating conditions. Mr. Lodhi has called the technology a “game changer”.

Members of the Armed Police Force of Nepal unload and prepare relief goods, including food, medicine and sanitary products, donated by local nonprofit Hami Nepal, to be transported via drone to stranded residents hit by deadly flash floods and mudslides across the Trishuli River in Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, September 8, 2026. REUTERS/Joseph Campbell | Photo Credit: Reuters

Recalling the use of mules, yaks and porters during the 2015 earthquakes in the Himalayan country, he said innovation and technology has ensured that food reaches those in need in five to 10 minutes. Mr. Lodhi said that WFP had not used drones at this scale before.

Nepal flood survivors join rescue and relief operations as they grieve, search for their loved ones

The WFP has said that it expects to provide food relief for four to six months in Nepal.

What is the road ahead?

The road to rebuilding Nepal is a long one. The access challenges are going to remain even as Nepali leaders say that the country is going to need long-term support. The country has estimated that the reconstruction bill will amount to $4.78 billion.

Himalayan tragedy points to need for new global alliances around ecological governance

“In living memory, we haven’t seen a mountain hazard event like this for a very, very long time,” Kamal Kishore, the Head of the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction said.

As climate change accelerates, concerns mount over safety of these regions in the Himalayan belt. Flash floods last year in the same region too had caused extensive damage and claimed nine lives. Experts have called for stricter norms, assessing infrastructure for multiple disasters, focusing on development in less-dangerous areas and early warning systems.

full_article:
KATHMANDU: Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Nepal Park Jae-kyung paid a courtesy call on Minister of Information and Communications Dr Bikram Timilsina at the latter’s office today.

During the meeting, they discussed Nepal-Korea relations, rescue, rehabilitation and assistance for victims of the Bhotekoshi floods, as well as cooperation in information technology, the digital economy and artificial intelligence.

Minister Timilsina expressed gratitude for Korea’s support and solidarity with Nepal during the difficult period following the Bhotekoshi floods. He thanked the Korean government for deploying a disaster response team for search and rescue operations and for its commitment to supporting flood victims and reconstruction and resettlement efforts.

Timilsina emphasized the need to further strengthen the friendly relations between Nepal and Korea based on mutual respect, understanding and cooperation.

Ambassador Park said Korea’s support for rescue and rehabilitation efforts in the flood-affected areas would continue. He also expressed concern about Korean citizens affected by the floods.

According to Park, a team of Korean security personnel has rescued 10 Korean citizens who were trapped by the floods, while nine Korean citizens in the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project area remain unaccounted for.

Park also informed Minister Timilsina about Nepal’s participation, along with other countries, in the 12th Global ICT Leadership Forum, which began in South Korea on Sept. 30.

The forum, organized by South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT and coordinated by the National Information Society Agency, features high-level discussions among representatives from various countries, including Nepal, on cooperation in information technology and artificial intelligence, as well as future strategies in these fields.

title: Nepal flash floods: Six bodies found in Upper Trishuli-1 tunnel search - India Today
description: Nepal flash floods: Six bodies found in Upper Trishuli-1 tunnel search  India Today
publisher.title: India Today
full_article:
Six bodies were recovered on Friday from a tunnel at a hydropower project in Nepal as search operations continued for people missing after last month’s devastating flash floods, which have killed more than 1,400 people and left over 6,100 untraced.

The bodies were found at the Upper Trishuli-1 project in Nuwakot district, while rescue teams kept searching other affected sites as roads linking key parts of the country also returned to regular two-way traffic.

The Nepal Army said a joint team of security forces recovered the bodies from the Audit-3 tunnel at the Upper Trishuli-1 project site. The bodies were found entangled in a steel reinforcement mesh prepared for concrete work inside the tunnel. According to Nepal Army Headquarters, the team used grinders, gas cutters and rotary rescue equipment to remove them.

The Bhotekoshi flash floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26. The floods devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal, killing at least 1,410 people and leaving 6,145 missing as of Thursday. Search and rescue teams have so far rescued more than 13,756 people from different affected areas.

Search operations have also been underway at several other hydropower projects, including Rasuwagadhi, Rasuwa Bhotekoshi, Langtang, Trishuli-3A and Upper Trishuli-3B. Meanwhile, the Tribhuvan and Kanti highways, the two main routes connecting Hetauda with Kathmandu, resumed regular two-way vehicular movement from Friday, according to Santosh Subedi, administrative officer at the District Administration Office in Makawanpur. The move followed the resumption of traffic at the Krishnabhir section of the Prithvi Highway in Dhading district, which had been blocked after the road collapsed following the August 26 floods.

The Tribhuvan Highway connects Hetauda with Kathmandu via Palung-Naubise, while the Kanti Highway connects the two cities via Tikabhairav-Lalitpur. Since September 1, goods carriers and large vehicles had been using the Tribhuvan Highway to reach Kathmandu and the Kanti Highway for the return journey to ensure smoother and safer traffic movement after the Prithvi Highway obstruction. With the Krishnabhir section now operational, both highways have been opened for regular two-way traffic, Subedi said.

The latest recovery at Upper Trishuli-1 underlined the continuing impact of the August 26 flash floods, with rescue teams still searching tunnels and project sites for the missing even as transport links in the affected areas are being restored.

title: Sri Lankan, Bangladeshi travel trade delegations affirm, 'Nepal is safe for tourism’ - The Tourism Times
description: Sri Lankan, Bangladeshi travel trade delegations affirm, 'Nepal is safe for tourism’  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: More than 150 tour and travel agents from Sri Lanka have arrived in Kathmandu to help spread a message to the world: Nepal is safe for tourism in the aftermath of the devastating Bhote Koshi floods.

Senior representatives of the Travel Agents Association of Sri Lanka (TAASL) and the IATA Agents Association of Sri Lanka (IAASL) have chosen Nepal as the venue for their annual general meetings.

The Sri Lankan delegation’s visit coincides with that of a 185-member corporate delegation from Bangladesh, representing Walton Plaza, which has also arrived in Kathmandu, reaffirming Nepal’s strong appeal as a destination for business and leisure travel, according to the Nepal Tourism Board.

Their visit reflects growing confidence among international travelers in Nepal and highlights the country’s welcoming hospitality, diverse experiences, and safe, accessible destinations. Such visits are also strengthening tourism and corporate ties with Nepal, the NTB said.

“Over 150 senior executives of the Sri Lankan travel and tour industries, representing TAASL and IAASL, are here in Kathmandu not only to hold the annual general meeting but mainly to join Nepal in this hour of grief,” said Sonali Ranasinghe, the first female president of TAASL.

As a neighboring country, Sri Lanka has always stood with Nepal, having faced many natural calamities itself in the past, Ranasinghe said, adding that their visit to Nepal was mainly aimed at spreading the message that Nepal is safe and needs more visitors now than ever.

Rohan Jayamanna, President of IAASL, said the delegation felt that Nepal remains a safe destination and one of the world’s best travel destinations. “TAASL and IAASL are always ready to join hands with Nepal-based tourism associations to promote both countries,” Jayamanna said, adding, “Sri Lanka considers Nepal a premier travel destination for its citizens.”

Sri Lankan Ambassador to Nepal Ruwanthi Delpitiya appreciated TAASL and IAASL’s efforts to bring leading Sri Lankan travel trade partners to Nepal. The ambassador also underscored the mutual recognition of untapped potential between the two South Asian nations. “Such visits certainly help foster stronger business linkages and investment prospects between the two countries,” she said, adding that Nepal could position Sri Lanka as a premier travel destination for its citizens. This would allow Nepalis to enjoy Sri Lanka’s spiritual sites, golden beaches, scenic hill country, wildlife safaris, and world-renowned wellness experiences.

Sunil Sharma, Deputy Director at the Nepal Tourism Board, emphasized that both nations could significantly expand their tourism promotion activities through such visits. “Nepal has always regarded Sri Lanka as one of its major tourist source markets, as the two countries share many bonds,” Sharma said.

Presenting Nepal’s tourism prospects, Sharma also highlighted the deep cultural and religious roots shared by the two nations. With both countries home to profound Buddhist and Hindu heritage, the delegation highlighted a unique opportunity to create a “spiritual circuit” for travelers. He also showcased Nepal’s diverse tourism experiences and MICE opportunities to the Sri Lankan travel fraternity.

Joy Dewan, President of the Nepal-Sri Lanka Friendship Association, thanked the travel delegations, saying their move meant something special to Nepal. “Nepal always views Sri Lanka not just as a neighbor, but as a strategic partner for mutual growth,” he added.

Sunil Shakya, an executive board member of NSLFA, described the visit by Sri Lankan trade leaders during this time of crisis as highly meaningful. “Nepal is fully safe for travel, which is why the delegation is here,” he said.

Bharat Jung Pandey, President of the Nepal Association of Tours and Travel Agents (NATTA), said bilateral tourism cooperation could market the two countries as a combined destination for pilgrimage, cultural exploration, and adventure. “NATTA is always ready to collaborate with TAASL and IAASL for tourism promotion,” he said.

The Sri Lankan delegation’s visit could also be described as a tourism confidence-building campaign for Nepal, said Ramesh Parajuli, Secretary of NATTA, whose company, Rupse Holidays, hosted the delegation locally. The presence of leading travel industry professionals from Sri Lanka reflects growing confidence in Nepal as a destination for international gatherings and business events, Parajuli noted.

By Adnan Abidi, Tyrone Siu and Sahana Bajracharya

BETRAWATI, Nepal/DEVIGHAT, Nepal, Sept 18 (Reuters) - Anusa Thapa Magar rushed home from her job in the Maldives after hearing about Nepal's devastating floods, hoping that her beloved grandmother was one of those who survived.

She headed for the family's two-storey house in ‌the small town of Betrawati.

But there was no house, and no Betrawati.

Those who escaped last month's disaster, when a torrent of mud and rocks swept across ‌the Nepal-China border area, have been returning to see what they can recover. In some cases, all they have found is a flat expanse of grey silt.

Standing on the hardened mud, the 23-year-old Magar wondered whether ​her grandmother, who could barely walk, was beneath the ground. "Aama" — mother, in Nepalese — was last seen resting on her bed.

"If my house is buried underneath, that means my Aama is still here underneath too, right?" said Magar.

Each day, scores of survivors sheltering in clusters of tents on a hillside above the site of Betrawati walk the half a kilometre (500 yards) to wander across the wasteland that was once their town, searching for traces of homes, shops and loved ones swallowed by the floods.

There are 5,130 people still reported missing on the Nepal side of the border ‌after the flood caused by a glacial collapse that swept ⁠down the mountains, killing at least 1,386 people. The authorities continue to search for survivors, but it has been days since anyone has been found alive.

A TRAIL OF PANIC

The highway linking Bidur to Betrawati has been replaced by a thick layer of mud deposited by ⁠the flood-swollen river.

Reaching Betrawati now requires climbing a steep hillside, traversing a narrow ridge and then descending into what had been a bustling settlement.

Along the way lie abandoned shoes and slippers, silent evidence of the panic that unfolded as people scrambled to escape the torrent of water, mud and rock. A deserted school building stands half-buried in debris. Further up the trail, children's shoes, ​school ​ties, and backpacks are scattered across the mud.

The floodwaters surged downstream with such force that they slammed ​into the base of a hill before rebounding across the valley, ‌sweeping away everything in their path.

Betrawati residents said warnings about the approaching flood began circulating minutes before it arrived, as friends and relatives upstream phoned to alert them. But few grasped the speed or scale of what was coming.

Garment business owner Kalpana Thapa Magar, 43, recalled receiving a call from a friend, telling her: "Run! Run!"

"I just ran. When I looked back, everything was gone, even the people who had been running behind me," she said.

In Devighat, downstream, partial shells of houses still stand. Residents have been salvaging what belongings they can, though many say they will have no reason to return again.

Madhav Ghimire, 42, carries the keys to the six-room house he shared with Ambika Aryal, 38, but ‌the landscape has changed so dramatically that they can no longer identify where it stood.

"Though I ​lost everything, I have still carried the keys of my home. It gives me a sense that ​I have everything," he said.

LOST EVERYTHING

For many families in the region, it was ​not the first disaster they had endured. Nearly 9,000 people were killed in Nepal's 2015 earthquake.

Teacher Sita Thapa Magar, 45, Kalpana's older sister, ‌said the earthquake had brought hardship and loss, but families had ​at least been able to salvage belongings and ​rebuild on their land. This time, the two houses she owned with her husband had been swept away and their farmland buried under debris.

"This time, we have lost everything," she said.

Shanti Dangol, 61, stood on a single broken tile, the only visible trace of her home, holding a photograph of the three-storey ​lodge that once stood there.

She described Betrawati as a once-thriving ‌town that catered to pilgrims and trekkers and had grown more prosperous in recent years as families built larger homes, rented rooms and invested in ​their children's education.

"Economically, people here had started doing well. Now, nothing remains," she said.
